subject: desert rock
title: What If 700-Pound Rocks Moved on Their Own? In Death Valley They Do

scenes.text: What if 700-pound rocks slid across a desert with nobody touching them? In Death Valley they do.
On a dry lake bed called Racetrack Playa, rocks leave trails hundreds of metres long. From the 1940s on, nobody ever saw one move.
The guesses: hurricane winds, dust devils, slippery algae. In 2011 two cousins fitted fifteen rocks with GPS and waited.
December 2013. Rare rain leaves a shallow pond. Overnight it freezes into ice as thin as a windowpane.
Around noon the sun cracks it into huge floating sheets, and a light wind pushes them against the rocks.
And the rocks sail, a few metres a minute. More than sixty moved in one day. Then they can sit still for a decade.

description:
What if 700-pound rocks moved across a desert on their own? At Racetrack Playa in Death Valley they do, and in 2014 scientists finally showed how.
A team led by Richard Norris of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography fitted 15 rocks with GPS in 2011 and, in December 2013, watched them move: a shallow pond froze overnight into thin windowpane ice, the morning sun broke it into large floating panels, and light winds of about 10 miles an hour pushed the ice against the rocks at 2 to 6 metres a minute. More than 60 rocks moved in a single event. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in August 2014.
